articles.text: The theme of Piedmont Community Church’s Mexico trip during Spring Break was building sanctuary – creating inclusivity, safety and a refuge for those around us, and the families for which we would build a home. We came together to erect 12 beautiful homes built by hand and without any power tools, outside of Tijuana in only four days. We built both physical and spiritual sanctuaries. Artificial hierarchies of ages and cliques vanished, and the beauty of our high schoolers shined through. The strength of our young women was on display as was the vulnerability of our young men. We created a space safe enough for all of us to be ourselves. We made concrete one batch at a time, and built every wall, raised rooves and installed doors. The Yellow Team, led by seniors Cole Anderson and Sophie Nevis, built a home for a six-person family that included two special needs adults, a three-year-old named Jose Luis, and their blind grandmother Rosa. Our days began at 6:30 a.m., leaving our tents to temperatures colder than one would expect in Mexico, at 40 degrees. Later in the day it would reach a perfect 75. After breakfast each day we drove our team vans to our building sites, with music blasting to hype us up. Once on site we held hands and thanked our families as we began our work. The homes we built were 11’ x 22,’ small by our standards, but enormous in value to our families. After arriving on Sunday, April 10, day one of work began Monday and included laying the concrete foundation by hand, which had to be level and perfectly sized to install seven walls later in the week. Levelling is sometimes no small feat. The Black Team required 50 cinderblocks to create a level surface. “With many members of our team being first-time volunteers, we fell behind on the first day. But we were eventually able to catch up with the help of our committed team, parent leader Doug Biehn and our hardworking rovers,” said Black Team leader,

articles.text: The inaugural Piedmont Food Fest is coming to town on Sunday, April 24, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., and there will be something for everyone at this food, drink, and musical showcase. The Food Fest team is seeking enthusiastic volunteers to help make this community event a success. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org/volunteer for details and come join the fun. The Food Fest has taken the whole village to come to life. In partnership with the city, schools, local businesses, community partners, and the fiscal sponsor Social Good, Piedmont Food Fest welcomes visitors to the family-friendly event. Come enjoy the food, stories of the people behind the food, locally sourced beer and wine, as well as multicultural stage performances, and a kid activity zone. If all goes well, this event may even turn into another annual tradition the community can look forward to year after year. A central mission of Piedmont Food Fest is to showcase the many diverse offerings of the broader Bay Area community that help enrich the experiences of our community and our neighbors. The event will feature food from Curry Up Now, Ceviche & Co, Swahili Spot, Kiss My Boba, Piedmont’s Robert Dorsey Catering, and others. Live music will be provided by the mariachi duo Son Nuestro, the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Black Music Incubator Showcase, and the Oakland Samba Revue. To register or volunteer, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org. While you’re there, be sure to check out the premium wine & beer tasting package, which includes a limited edition tumbler while supplies last.
articles.title: Piedmont Food Fest comes to town this Sunday

If we look at Piedmont’s AP scores and SAT/ACT scores, it’s clear that our education isn’t being squandered, we are still outperforming schools nationwide. We are still an academic As for CAASPP testing, I have no doubt they’re terrible scores, I have yet to meet a student who put effort into doing it. The sad truth is, if it’s not worth a grade, it’s not worth the time. And that is absolutely an issue and I have no problem saying it. But it demonstrates moreso how culturally we’re lagging behind the rest of the world. articles.text: To help inform the City’s next iteration of reach code development, members of the city staff have launched a public engagement process. The first component entails a survey. The city requests Piedmont residents and those who work in town to complete an online survey to provide feedback about the current reach codes with suggestions for the next round. The online survey is live and will be open until May 20. The link to the survey is: https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/reach_code_information. All those who complete the online survey will be enrolled in a raffle to receive a bill credit from Piedmont’s local electricity service provider, East Bay Community Energy (EBCE). Reach code forum tonight at 6 p.m. The second component of the engagement process will be an in-person Reach Code Community Forum tonight, April 20, from 6:00 to 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. City staff will present an overview of Piedmont’s current reach codes, the 2022 Energy Code, and initial considerations for the next set of reach codes, followed by a community workshop where attendees will be asked to provide comments and recommendations about the current and future code. While not required, registration for the in-person event is strongly encouraged at: https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FAIpQLSfzsKAQ32t2hhk59XZIlC8k83R8GTjocs_EvbkIQygjQmr4UQ/viewform. All those attending the Reach Code Forum will be entered into a raffle to win a free energy savings kit and EBCE bill credit. For more information about the reach codes and upcoming events, please visit the City’s Reach Code Information webpage. Additional information about building electrification, rebates, resources, and incentives available for Piedmonters can be found at: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/electrification. For questions, contact the City Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman.

articles.text: Friday is deadline to restore Prop 58 and Prop 193 The California Association of Realtors ran a costly, misleading campaign in November 2020 which pushed through the passage of Proposition 19 by a 51% margin. The ads touted expanding portability across all counties for seniors, the disabled, and wildfire victims by permitting relocation to new homes while retaining their tax base. But the ads failed to mention Prop 19’s “Death Tax.” April 22, 2022 – Friday this week – is the deadline for submitting 1,000,000 valid signatures to get the “Repeal the Death Tax” initiative on November’s ballot and to the voters. Many voters at the time were distracted amidst the global pandemic, endless smoky wildfires, shelter-in-place, and the struggle to run a free and fair presidential election. Prop 19 amended the state constitution by effectively removing Prop 58 and 193 protections which allowed parents the ability to transfer property of any value to their children without triggering reassessments and without increasing market-driven taxes. The same protection for grandparent to grandchildren transfers were also removed by Prop 19. The working class will suffer the most, as Prop 19 also eliminated any exemption of taxable value for other property. Increased food insecurity, challenges in retaining staff, higher rents or forced evictions will result. Prop 19 is terrible for California. My husband, Daniel Riddle, and I have taken efforts to restore Prop 58 and 193 protections that Californians overwhelmingly voted for. articles.text: The City of Piedmont published its draft report of the 6th Cycle Housing Element for 2023- 2031 on April 8. It considers new land uses, housing types, building types, heights, residential density, code changes, and other housing-related initiatives and policies that aim to accommodate nearly 600 new units by 2031. All Bay Area local governments have until January 2023 to update their Housing Elements. Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee Chair Rani Batra encouraged all Piedmont residents and other stakeholders to participate in upcoming public meetings, as well as share their thoughts on the draft Housing Element. “We can all look forward to seeing the public review draft of the Housing Element and then being able to engage together on it at three different public forums this spring,” she said. “We really appreciate hearing [community] voices.” The next Planning Commission public hearing will be held on May 12 at 5:30 p.m. Residents may also email comments to the city at PiedmontisHome@piedmont. ca.gov, or mail them to ‘Draft Housing Element, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611.’ “It is going to take all of us to make room for more housing in Piedmont,” Batra said. Piedmont declined to appeal its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA), which requires the city to make room for 587 affordable housing units. These can be in the form of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), Junior Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs), and lot-splitting; as well as finding parcels of land where more dense housing could be developed. Nearly every city in California received a higher RHNA in the next housing cycle, and many have appealed their allocations before the end of 2021. The Housing Element does not require the city to physically increase its housing stock; instead, it is meant to provide an analysis of development constraints and the immediate and long-terms housing needs in the city. The Element must also identify land and financial resources that will meet the city’s RHNA, establish policies that address those needs, and include programs that would help implement those policies. “Our Housing Element holds the key to many issues including our approaches to housing, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, transportation, educational opportunity, and others. Housing is fundamental to the health and well-being of any community, including Piedmont,” explained Mayor Teddy Gray King. The city projects that City Council will review the Housing Element this summer, and the City will then submit it to the state for review in late summer. Piedmont is targeting a Housing Element 2023 - 2031 adoption by May 2023. Comments from public Unattributed comments collected from community workshops and focus groups between July 2021 and March 2022 are included in the draft Housing Element. A key finding was that an average Piedmont household has an income more than double the Alameda County average, with a median household income of $224,659. One community workshop participant was quoted, “I work in Piedmont, but cannot afford to live in the city.” Another comment stated, “we need affordable housing for firefighters, city staff, and teachers.” Public comment reflected an interest in small (400 sq-foot) units to accommodate students and young professionals, more housing for seniors, more mixed-use housing developments (commerce and residential), and smaller homes (less than 2,000 sq. ft.). Those who attended public meetings and provided comment before the draft Element was released also stated that there is a need to include voices outside of Piedmont, and that there is a need to change negative perceptions and assumptions about affordable housing and density. The draft document also reports that a large portion of Piedmont residents, both renters and homeowners, are cost-burdened, meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on housing and bills. Additionally, the analysis, prepared by Lisa Wise Consulting, noted that Piedmont seniors have few options to “downsize” and agein-place; whereas families with young children have found it difficult to find their “starter home” in Piedmont. Read the draft in full at www. piedmontishome.org.

articles.text: As spring has sprung, we see flowers and fruits pop up all around us. What about Earth makes it so special for growing so many plants? Earth is unique because it has the conditions needed to support life: air, water, and sunlight (temperature). Earth’s atmosphere has Carbon Dioxide gas; which plants rely on for photosynthesis. The water cycle provides freshwater for plants via rainfall, lakes, and groundwater. The planet’s approximate distance from the sun provides energy and comfortable temperatures for plants to thrive in as well. Plants that are adapted to survive within Earths’ conditions might not do so well in foreign environments. The Moon has no atmosphere, which means it is exposed to the extreme conditions of space. There is no air, no liquid water, and unreliable temperatures. The soil is mostly rock and dust, which provides little to no nutrients for healthy plant growth. Mars has an atmosphere that is very different from Earth’s, with 96% being Carbon Dioxide gas. The average temperature on Mars is -81°F, which is too cold for plants and there is no liquid water that we know of. Its soil is rich in iron-oxides which gives the planet its rusty, red color, but missing many of the essential minerals and nutrients required for plant growth. As astronauts plan missions to the Moon and Mars, they must think about how to provide plants with these vital resources when there are none. Both of these environments have new, unexpected, and unexperienced challenges for plant growth. In order to investigate what resources plants need to grow, try an experiment on sprouting beans. Adult supervision is recommended throughout this 7. Together, make some predictions about the beans: • How long do you think it will take for them to start growing? • Do you think they will all grow the same rate, size, etc.? 8. Each day for the next 7-10 days, check on the beans. Record observations and track their growth using the data sheet. Ask some of the following questions: • What do you notice about the beans? • What do you notice about the environment inside the bag? • Are they all growing the same? Which beans are growing more, or less, and why do you think that is? 9. Determine what plants need to survive based on the results of your experiment. Discuss some of the following ideas to expand further: • How do you think the beans grow without soil? • What are some of the differences between Earth and The Moon? Or Mars? • What resources might be missing on The Moon or Mars? Water, air, sunlight, and soil are some of the main ingredients needed to grow healthy crops. Haley Thiltgen is an Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center, is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. Chabot is located at 10,000 Skyline Boulevard in Oakland. Bean sprouts experiment. Bean seeds are small and easy to swallow. 1. Gather your learners and the materials needed: • Bean seeds: lima beans, pinto beans, lentil beans, or mung beans work well • Cotton Balls or Paper • Towels • Plastic Bags (small-medium) • Water • Bowl for water • Tape • Window (or place with good lighting) • Marker • Writing utensil • Ruler (optional) 2. Begin with a discussion, using some of the questions below: • What do plants need to grow? • What about Earth makes it so special for growing plants? • Do you think a plant could survive without water, air, sun, or soil? 3. Give everyone a plastic bag and label them with a permanent marker. 4. Fill a bowl with water. Dip a few cotton balls or paper towels into the water and place them into the plastic bag. 5. Next, add 2-3 beans into each bag. Be careful not to overfill the bag. 6. Tape the bag up on a window, or a place with plenty of light.

articles.text: High drama in warmup for World Championship in Houston Charlie Lambert (left) and Vaughn Khouri place Selkie before a match. Seventeen students from Highlander Robotics, Piedmont High School’s robotics team, traveled with their robot “Selkie” to San Jose State on April 8 to compete as one of 59 teams from as far away as the Dominican Republic in the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Silicon Valley Regional Tournament. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season. In this year’s game, Rapid React, robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inch-wide tennis balls into an 8-foot high 4-footwide funnel before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. FRC Tournaments, which frame robotics as a sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, consist of a day of practice matches, a day and a half of qualification matches, and half a day of playoffs with alliances formed through a draft system. Teams expect to compete in 9 to 12 qualifying rounds with 30-60 minute breaks in between, leaving little time for repairs in an atmosphere akin to F1 Racing. The Highlanders were coming off success at the Sacramento Regional where they qualified for the World Championship in Houston next week. In San Jose they looked to refine their robot and skill, but ran into problems early into practice matches when a belt on their drive train broke and they found themselves without a spare. “Typically, we can borrow parts when that happens” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark, “but this particular belt was more obscure than we’d anticipated, and I thought we might be going home that night,” he added. Thankfully a spare was eventually found by another team and Selkie was back up and running. In the fast-paced and high-scoring qualifying rounds, the Highlanders went 7-2 and finished 11th of 59 teams. In one round the two sides were so capable that the number of balls scored confused the field sensors, causing miscounts and requiring a rematch. In the playoffs, The Highlanders were selected by 4th seed RoboDores from Monterey and advanced to the best-of-three quarterfinals against an alliance captained by 5th seed Berkelium from Berkeley. In the first round, the opposition fielded only two robots due to mechanical issues and they opted to use the round to go back to their pit for repairs. The result seemed to be a foregone conclusion until Selkie’s intake, part of the robot that extends to pick up balls, got caught on Berkelium’s intake. The round devolved into a tug of war across the field in an effort to prevent one another from scoring points or forcing penalties. The Highlanders won 83 to 59 but in the process bent a piston on their intake. Twenty seconds into second round match, Selkie’s main breaker blew and it was left immobile after a solid hit by Jump Robotics. That match ended 56 to 65. With less than 20 minutes until the quarterfinal tie breaker, the Highlander pit crew flew into action: replacing the breaker, fixing the bent piston, and running pre-match checks. With less than two minutes remaining for Selkie to enter the field or be disqualified, it was discovered that a vital sensor had been damaged. With no time to return to the pit, the team duct taped the sensor casing and hoped for the best. As the round started, teammates in the stands let out a collective sigh of relief as it was clear that the damaged sensor was still working and Selkie began racking up points. With 30 seconds left and a 10-point lead, a part on Selkie’s intake failed and the robot was unable to pick up any more balls. The match ended in a 83-83 tie and Berkeley’s alliance won based on tie break rules. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Charlie Lambert, technician Nate Hart, and human player Arun Brahma. Alex Ware led the pit crew which kept the robot running. Jasper Tripp and Charlie Clowes ran scouting operations which informed alliance selection for the playoffs. Chloe Kessinger and Lewy Seiden acted as team ambassadors, answering questions, building connections with other teams, and representing the team to FIRST Judges. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is now comprised of 31 students from four schools – Piedmont High, College Prep, Las Lomas, and Head Royce. For more information contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com. Highland Robotics robot Selkie (#8033), shoots nine and a half inch tennis balls at an eight-foot-high funnel.

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, April 20, 2022 Highlander Robotics tests its mettle in San Jose High drama in warmup for World Championship in Houston Charlie Lambert (left) and Vaughn Khouri place Selkie before a match. Seventeen students from Highlander Robotics, Piedmont High School’s robotics team, traveled with their robot “Selkie” to San Jose State on April 8 to compete as one of 59 teams from as far away as the Dominican Republic in the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Silicon Valley Regional Tournament. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season. In this year’s game, Rapid React, robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inch-wide tennis balls into an 8-foot high 4-footwide funnel before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. FRC Tournaments, which frame robotics as a sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, consist of a day of practice matches, a day and a half of qualification matches, and half a day of playoffs with alliances formed through a draft system. Teams expect to compete in 9 to 12 qualifying rounds with 30-60 minute breaks in between, leaving little time for repairs in an atmosphere akin to F1 Racing. The Highlanders were coming off success at the Sacramento Regional where they qualified for the World Championship in Houston next week. In San Jose they looked to refine their robot and skill, but ran into problems early into practice matches when a belt on their drive train broke and they found themselves without a spare. “Typically, we can borrow parts when that happens” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark, “but this particular belt was more obscure than we’d anticipated, and I thought we might be going home that night,” he added. Thankfully a spare was eventually found by another team and Selkie was back up and running. In the fast-paced and high-scoring qualifying rounds, the Highlanders went 7-2 and finished 11th of 59 teams. In one round the two sides were so capable that the number of balls scored confused the field sensors, causing miscounts and requiring a rematch. In the playoffs, The Highlanders were selected by 4th seed RoboDores from Monterey and advanced to the best-of-three quarterfinals against an alliance captained by 5th seed Berkelium from Berkeley. In the first round, the opposition fielded only two robots due to mechanical issues and they opted to use the round to go back to their pit for repairs. The result seemed to be a foregone conclusion until Selkie’s intake, part of the robot that extends to pick up balls, got caught on Berkelium’s intake. The round devolved into a tug of war across the field in an effort to prevent one another from scoring points or forcing penalties. The Highlanders won 83 to 59 but in the process bent a piston on their intake. Twenty seconds into second round match, Selkie’s main breaker blew and it was left immobile after a solid hit by Jump Robotics. That match ended 56 to 65. With less than 20 minutes until the quarterfinal tie breaker, the Highlander pit crew flew into action: replacing the breaker, fixing the bent piston, and running pre-match checks. With less than two minutes remaining for Selkie to enter the field or be disqualified, it was discovered that a vital sensor had been damaged. With no time to return to the pit, the team duct taped the sensor casing and hoped for the best. As the round started, teammates in the stands let out a collective sigh of relief as it was clear that the damaged sensor was still working and Selkie began racking up points. With 30 seconds left and a 10-point lead, a part on Selkie’s intake failed and the robot was unable to pick up any more balls. The match ended in a 83-83 tie and Berkeley’s alliance won based on tie break rules. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Charlie Lambert, technician Nate Hart, and human player Arun Brahma. Alex Ware led the pit crew which kept the robot running. Jasper Tripp and Charlie Clowes ran scouting operations which informed alliance selection for the playoffs. Chloe Kessinger and Lewy Seiden acted as team ambassadors, answering questions, building connections with other teams, and representing the team to FIRST Judges. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is now comprised of 31 students from four schools – Piedmont High, College Prep, Las Lomas, and Head Royce. For more information contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com. Highland Robotics robot Selkie (#8033), shoots nine and a half inch tennis balls at an eight-foot-high funnel. articles.text: PHS athlete has second-highest decathlon score in U.S. Parker Terrill won the Del Campo Decathlon in Fair Oaks near Sacramento on Saturday. Piedmont senior Parker Terrill proved he’s much more than a one-event athlete. The recent holder of a new school record in the pole vault at 15-feet, 5-inches, on Saturday he added nine more events and won the decathlon with a score that is second best in the U.S. He ran, threw, and jumped his way to a first-place finish in a field of 12 at the Del Campo Decathlon on Friday and Saturday, April 15-16, at Fair Oaks High School near Sacramento. His 5,964 total points for the 10 events was the second-highest decathlon score in the country this year behind Kaden Passey of Team Shadow Ridge in Arizona. At the Terrill eclipsed Piedmont’s all-time pole vault mark, he said that his prime focus was improving as a complete athlete for the decathlon. Last weekend he provided some proof. At Del Campo he notched personal bests in the 400 and 1500 meters, in addition to the shot put, high jump, and long jump. “I just really wanted to get all my personal records and lifetime bests, and I got five of them. It’s been really fun to see it come all together,” he said. At Del Campo, he defeated Axel Verdoorn of Pleasant Grove in Sacramento by 400 points, and Collin Friedman of El Camino in Sacramento by 600 points. The decathlon is scored by performance in 10 events instead of overall finish. Running events include the 100, 400, and 1500 meter runs, in addition to the 110- meter hurdles. Throwing events are the shot, discus, and javelin, while the jumping events include the high jump, long jump, and Terrill’s specialty, the pole vault. “What matters most is the distance you threw or time you ran. There is some strategy with priority in different events. Throws are pretty significant because they are the first events. Jumps are also significant; points and are based upon how difficult the events are,” explained Terrill.
articles.title: Parker Terrill wins Del Campo Decathlon

articles.text: Photo courtesy of FIFA.com The 2022 World Cup Draw is out with the United States in Group B with England and Iran, and Wales facing Ukraine or Scotland to play in. The list of teams for each group in the 2022 World Cup was announced on April 4. The United States is in Group B with England, Iran, and the European playoff winner between Wales and Ukraine or Scotland. Instead of the usual July start for the 92-year-old tournament, this year’s World Cup will be played in the winter months due to the excessive summer heat of Qatar, the host country located on the Persian Gulf. Group stage matches will be played November 21 through December 2, with the Round of 16 December 3-6, and quarterfinals on December 9-10. The World Cup semifinal games will be played December 13-14, with the third-place game on December 17 and the championship game on December 18. The U.S. men’s team currently is ranked No. 15 and is the second-highest team in the group behind England at No. 5. If Wales (No. 18) or Ukraine (No. 27) qualify, Group B will be the only group with all four teams in the world’s top-30. Scotland, meanwhile, is no cookie at No. 39 overall. The U.S. and England are set to play the day after Thanksgiving, Friday, November 25, and could be the most-watched U.S. Men’s team game of all time. Provided below is a primer for each team and its key players. England The Three Lions of England are the hands down favorite to win the Group B. Their only loss in a year and a half was on a penalty shootout with Italy in the UEFA Euro Finals on July 11. British fans will undoubtedly have high expectations that the cup will be “coming home” to the argued birthplace of European football. England has a roster of superstars led by Tottenham striker Harry Kane, who has 49 international goals in 69 appearances for England. Other star players who could make the squad include Manchester City’s Raheem Sterling, Jack Grealish, and Phil Foden, Arsenal’s Bukayo Saka, Manchester United Marcus Rashford and Jadon Sancho, and Chelsea’s Mason Mount. If England has any weakness it’s at center back and goalkeeper. Their top choice at CB is Man. United’s Harry Maguire, who is an accident waiting to happen. At keeper, Leicester’s Jordan Pickford likely remains the first choice, but hasn’t been in good form this year. Iran Iran will head into Group B as the biggest underdog. A player to keep an eye on is goalkeeper Alireza Beiranvand, who is more akin to an Olympic Discus thrower. He holds the Guinness World Record for a long-toss in an official match at an estimated 61.26 meters (67 yards). They’ll likely draw a solid crowd of supporters in Qatar. Wales, Ukraine/Scotland On June 5, Wales will face the winner of the Ukraine vs. Scotland match on June 1. Wales’ roster has talent in several top divisions of Europe. Real Madrid’s Gareth Bale, at 32, is a legendary goal scorer and plays at a more inspired level when with his national team. Leeds’ Daniel James is a pacey forward, while Tottenham’s Ben Davies provides a veteran leadership on the backline. Ukraine could become quite the story with the ongoing war with Russia. It’s still unclear if the current situation will prevent them from even competing after postponing the original March 24 play-in against Scotland. Their team has quite the roster with West Ham’s Andriy Yarmolenko, Man. City’s Oleksandr Zinchenko, and Benfica striker Roman Yaremchuk. Scotland will have a strong defense with Liverpool’s Andy Robertson and Arsenal’s Kieran Tierney, and talented midfielders Man. United’s Scott McTominay and Aston Villa’s John McGinn. My prediction would be for Wales to make it into Group B. United States So how does the United States shape up? This is perhaps the most talented U.S. team all time, with players who could represent the USA over the next eight years. There are no excuses for this team to not succeed, with a wealth of players in the top divisions of Europe, to include Chelsea’s Christian Pulisic, Juventus’ Weston McKennnie, RB Leipzig’s Tyler Adams, Dotrmund’s Gio Reyna, and RB Salzburg’s Brenden Aaronson. My early prediction is the United States finishes second to England with wins over Wales and Iran.

By Jonathan Comeaux The list of teams for each group in the 2022 World Cup was announced on April 4. Instead of the usual July start for the 92-year-old tournament, this year’s World Cup will be played in the winter months due to the excessive summer heat of Qatar, the host country located on the Persian Gulf. Group stage matches will be played November 21 through December 2, with the Round of 16 December 3-6, and quarterfinals on December 9-10. Staff Photos Hikers can still spot the char marks from fires from previous decades along the first- and second-generation redwoods in Portola State Park. The Old Big Tree at the end of the Old Tree Trail is estimated to be a 1,200-year- old redwood 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter. year old tree is among the few old growths to survive the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent for nearly two miles with an elevation gain of 550 feet. Upon intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail, turn left to start a loop trail back to your car at Peter’s Creek. Turning right begins a 1.5 mile-hike to an historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles with 500 feet in elevation gain to the end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when sharing the trail with other hikers. If you turn left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with Upper Escape Road. Turn right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car, making it a 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that we crossed 18 hikers on the 0.6 out-and-back Old Tree Trail. Those numbers would be larger if the campgrounds were open, given its popularity with young families. Aside from towering redwoods visible in every direction, you can often spot chickadees chirping about, an occasional banana slug wriggling beneath you, and the knocking of woodpeckers in the distance. Also closed in the park are the Coyote Ridge and Pomponio trails due to wildfires. The Iverson Trail on the way to Tiptoe Falls is also closed. However, the brief walk to the Pascadero Creek is open. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company’s production of Hotter Than Egypt ends this Sunday, April 24, and tickets are still available. The show, written by Yussef El Guindi and directed by John Langs, was selected by MTC’s new Associate Artistic Director Nakissa Etemad. It received its world premiere in a co-production with ACT in Seattle. This play follows protagonist couple Paul and Jean as they travel to Cairo, Egypt for their 24th wedding anniversary. Long-standing troubles within their marriage start to percolate, and their two Egyptian tour guides, newly engaged Maha and Seif, become entwined in the crisis. The play, which the writer describes as a “dramedy,” is set in the aftermath of the Egyptian revolution and explores the uneven power dynamics between these Western tourists and the locals. The cast members include Paul Morgan Stetler, Wasim No’mani Seif, Naseem Etemad, Jen Taylor, and Ahmad Kamal. articles.text: At the close of its 2022 season, San Francisco Ballet will honor the 37-year tenure of its Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson who retires this summer. A special gala performance will take place this Sunday, April 24, at 5:30 p.m. at the War Memorial Opera House. For the event, Tomasson has hand-selected ballets from the more than 50 works he choreographed and directed for San Francisco Ballet. Program includes The Fifth Season, Two Bits, Pas de Deux from Handel, pas de deux from Romeo and Juliet, and an excerpt from Harmony. Tomasson was a distinguished dancer before assuming artistic leadership of San Francisco Ballet in 1985. Under his direction, the Ballet became a company widely recognized as one of the finest in the world. He has cho- ® Photo courtesy of San Francisco Ballet Helgi Tomasson, Artist Director of SF Ballet reographed more than 50 works for the Company, including fulllength productions of Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, Romeo and Juliet (taped for Lincoln Center at the Movies’ Great American Dance), Giselle, and The Nutcracker (taped for PBS’s Great Performances). Tomasson has also connected San Francisco Ballet to the world through co-commissions with American Ballet Theatre, The Royal Ballet, and Dutch National Ballet; and major tours to Paris, London, New York City, China, and his native Iceland. In 2020, Tomasson was nominated to receive the San Francisco Arts Medallion, created by the Museum of Performance and Design to recognize individuals whose leadership, action, and generosity have benefited the cultural life of the San Francisco Bay Area. “Helgi is a visionary whose creativity, brilliance, and stewardship of the Ballet is reflected both in the caliber of the Company’s work, as well as in the thoughtful transition plan that he helped conceive to support the organization’s ongoing vitality,” said Sunnie Evers, Co-Chair of the SF Ballet Board. In her first solo exhibition, Auerbach showed a series of text-based drawings that explored various linguistic systems that included calligraphy, Morse code, semaphore signals, the Ugaritic alphabet and Alexander Melville Bell’s visible speech. The title of the exhibition, “S v Z” is a reference to the close Artist Tauba Auerbach yet indeterminate relationship between form and meaning that surfaces throughout the artist’s materials. articles.text: Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band brings some of the East Bay’s finest musicians to the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a show on Saturday, April 23. A 2008 graduate of Piedmont High School and Berklee College of Music in Boston four years later, Leyhe’s career has included performances with legendary musicians Buddy Guy, Jimmie Vaughan, Huey Lewis, Chris Cain, Charlie Musselwhite, and Fantastic Negrito. Come be part of an intimate evening of music at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 29 at 7 p.m. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. articles.text: Classical music and Hollywood film composer Erich Korngold. The tawdry spectacle of the most recent Academy Awards accomplished many things. I’m glad to have missed it. Hollywood is a fantasy world onto itself. I’d liken its history to a parabola – with humble beginnings, then the brilliance of music during the Weimar Republic fructified Hollywood. In its present state, Hollywood has regressed into the Stone Age… And that’s being generous. The excellent book Exiles in Hollywood by David Wallace gives a fine overview of the events. Many musicians went to Hollywood because of the lure of the almighty dollar. Stravinsky, in particular, was attracted by the dollar sign. He didn’t have a kind word to say about Hollywood in general, but the money more than made up for it. Rachmaninoff was the exact opposite. He liked the weather in California but rejected everything that Hollywood represented. Others, like George Gershwin, sought legitimacy. And so it was with many musicians. What is so interesting about the entire scene is that all of the exiles maintained close and friendly relations. There were the philosophers, and the writers, and every kind of Hollywood big shot and musicians all over the place. My aunt was the personal secretary to the writer Thomas Mann, and my parents knew the entire Otto Klemperer family. Two of the most interesting musicians of the era were the composers Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Erich Zeisl. Both were born in Vienna around the turn-of-the-century. Korngold had a most sensational childhood and arrived in Hollywood before the catastrophe struck Europe. Zeisl and his wife escaped just in the nick of time. Mrs. Zeisl was my Latin teacher during my days at Palisades High School in the early 1960s. Even though there was some talk about her late husband, I was too shy to ask her about him. Hollywood has always been fickle and duplicitous. But we must not lose sight of the great things that exist. Music composer for Hollywood films Erich Zeisl. The paths of the two great composers took completely different trajectories. Korngold arrived in Hollywood as an acclaimed genius. His compositions radically changed Hollywood filmmaking. Virtually every composer in Hollywood has benefited from his genius. Every Korngold score was a musical masterpiece and can stand on its own in the concert hall. Things aren’t like that anymore. But Hollywood was fickle, and Korngold was declared old-fashioned and unnecessary. He resumed writing for the concert hall and longed to return to Vienna. He did both. The other Erich, his friend Erich Zeisl, also was from Vienna. Zeisl’s struggle for acclaim was more arduous. His fame did not precede him. Nonetheless, he found lucrative employment in Hollywood, but he did not find fame. He was assigned hack work and usually did not get any screen credits. Considering his abilities and talent, his treatment was shameful. But he had no regrets and neither did his esteemed colleague, Korngold. Hollywood sure knew how to make great talents disappear. That’s what happened to the two Erichs. Too many things in life are treated as transitory. Great art should not be among these. If you are bored with the drivel that Hollywood turns out these days, listen to the scores of real geniuses like Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Erich Zeisl. Nothing can be more inspiring.

articles.text: Come join your friends for some laughs and libations when the Knockabouts improv comedy troupe comes to town – Saturday, April 30 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Tickets are $20 at https://bit. ly/3jDdi4W. The doors open at 7:15 p.m. and the show starts at 8:00 pm. Vaccine cards and masks required. A bit of background • Brian Molyneaux started his training in improv at The Second City back in Chicago and several years of dramatic acting as well. He has continued with his passion over the years and has performed with multiple groups of great improvisers. In addition to improvisation and acting, Brian is an acclaimed commercial photographer and director, a vocalist and a Piedmont dad of two wonderful daughters. • Joe Liss has been called “The Improviser’s Improviser.” He wrote and performed as a member of The Second City in Chicago. Joe’s comedic talent and character work is well known. You’ve seen him on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, Curb Your Enthusiasm, Strangers With Candy, and in Home Alone 2. He is the founder and Artistic Director of Morpho Theater in Oakland. • Lisa Martinovic is a writer who developed her performance chops on the poetry slam circuit during the 90s. Early in the 21st century she took up improv and has performed with three theater companies over the past 20 years: Magic Jester, Oaktown and Morpho.

articles.text: Dan Flanagan is a Berkeley violinist who currently teaches violin at UC Berkeley, is Principal Second of the Berkeley Symphony, Concertmaster of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera, Concertmaster of West Edge Opera, and performs with the San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Ballet. He has previously performed as concertmaster with Oakland Symphony, California Symphony, Symphony San Jose, Santa Rosa Symphony, California Musical Theater, Modesto Symphony, and Opera Parallele. He has performed recitals at the Piedmont Center for the Arts multiple times. Dan has been an avid collector since he discovered baseball cards at the age of five. He lost interest in them as a teenager but with the advent of Ebay when he was in grad school, he amassed an impressive collection of historical violinist memorabilia. When he moved to Berkeley 12 years ago, he discovered art auctions and open studios; that’s when the real trouble started. Since then his focus has been French Impressionists and Bay Area abstracts. The works on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts include 45 of his favorite pieces. Many of the artists were in the original Impressionist exhibits of the 1870’s and 1880’s. Dan has a project titled “The Bow and the Brush,” where he performs new compositions inspired by paintings. Two of these pieces were performed in the Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert series on April 10. Twenty-one of these works, each inspired by paintings currently exhibited at the Piedmont Center for the Arts ere, will be premiered by Dan at his Carnegie Hall debut on October 3, followed by the West Coast premieres at Hertz Hall in Berkeley on October 16. Robert Antoine Pinchon (French, 1886-1943). Bruxelles, pluie sur la Grand-Place (Brussels, rain on the Grand-Place), Oil on canvas, 1928. Jose Gonzalez Garcia composed “Cadenza II,” inspired by this painting.

Patten’s powerful artwork shines a light on Native American tribal culture. His rise to success started with a Christmas present in 2021, when his wife bought him an easel and some paints. “I have been in art all my life, but never had time to do art,” he said recently. “I haven’t been painting very long. I used to doddle, it always came out nice, but that was the extent of it. In the first week [with the easel] I must have put out 10 to 15 paintings. I just started pushing them out. articles.text: Encanto, released in theaters in 2021, and now streaming on Disney+, was the winner of the Oscar for Best Animated Feature Film. It has surged in popularity, a musical fantasy with eight songs written by Lin-Manuel Miranda (Hamilton) and has been compared to the remarkable Frozen. Since it appeared it has become a cultural phenom. It tells the tale of an extraordinary, extended, magical Latino family, headed by a 75-year-old matriarch, abuela Alma (Maria Cecelia Botero), who was forced to flee her home with her triplets due to violence that killed her husband Pedro. Because of the suffering she endured, Alma was granted magical powers that are bestowed on her family, to include a sentient house – a casita, located on the side of a hill in the town of Encanto, where the floorboards, staircase, and shutters pulse and throb. In the first song, “The Madrigal Family,” we are introduced to the clan. Each member has passed through a coming-of-age ritual in which they discover their own magical power, also called a “gift.” Emotional Pepa (Carolina Gaitan) can control the weather; beautiful Isabella (Diane Guerrero) can make flowers bloom; sensible Julieta (Angie Cepedal) can heal with her cooking; and Luisa (Jessica Darrow) can lift things. Everyone lives happily in the casita, except for Mirabel (Stephanie Beatriz), a 15-years-old, who is the only member of the family not to receive a special gift. Mirabel is crestfallen, for she realizes that it is the magical powers of the Madrigals that is the source of the community’s continuity. But improbably, it is Mirabel who begins to notice that the foundation of the casita is cracking, and Alma sees that their magic candle is growing dimmer. However, the Madrigals disregard their concerns. As it turns out, it will be up to Mirabel to restore her family’s magic. This effort will involve her uncle Bruno (John Leguizano), the family’s black sheep (conveyed through the song “We Don’t Talk About Bruno”) who can see the future and always tells the truth, no matter how scary. Family, however dysfunctional, is the essence of Encanto, and represents the essential life force, despite each member of the Madrigals secretly feeling the weight of their gift. Luisa, for example, sings the song “Surface Pressure” that expresses the burdensome demands that are made of her. The narrative point made, in so many ways, is that people are worthy because of who they are and not what they do. The challenge is to see your family members for who they really are. The visuals of Encanto are extraordinary, lush and compelling. And there are countless, intimate close-ups of Mirabel, whose emotions consist of bespectacled expressions that convey this smiling tale of family reconciliation. Encanto. Directed by Jared Bush and Byron Howard. With voices of Stephanie Beatriz, Maria Cecilia Botero, and Diane Guerrero. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2021. Now streaming on Disney+.

articles.text: One of my favorite wine tastings of the year is the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting in San Francisco which was held this year at the Palace Hotel on March 27. Zinfandel is not really native to California. Most ampelographers from UC Davis now believe it came to California from Croatia in the 1800s, but it’s certainly the trademark grape of the state. There was even a bill before the state legislature to declare it the official state wine (the Cabernet and Pinot producers protested). Ninety nine percent of the world’s Zinfandel is grown in California and because there is no French equivalent, it is the closest thing we have to a native son. World class Zinfandels are still much less expensive than world class California Cabernets, but unfortunately the price is edging upward. Most of the wines listed below retail for between $25 and $45. These wines can often be found at lower prices at places like the Wine Club in SF or on Wine.com. A note about my prejudices: I like Zinfandels that are fruitladen, big bodied, intense and rich. However it is also important to me that they have acid and structure and not be overblown fruit bombs. I am no fan of the lean and mean “finesse” Zinfandels. (If I want finesse I’ll drink Pinot Noir). Also, I have chosen not to write about the two best known and masterful Zin producers Ridge, and Ravenswood, as most wine lovers already know how great their wines are. Instead, I have sought out lesser-known producers who are doing an outstanding job. The wines below are the cream of this years Zinfandel crop. • 2019 Wilson Zinfandel Reserve, $32 The Wilson Family of wineries makes many outstanding Zinfandels and in the past I have highlighted Mazzocco and St. Anne’s Crossing. This year I was delighted with the 2019 Wilson Reserve Zin. It shows powerful, sweet aromas of ripe black cherries, boysenberries and currants, w i t h s u b - tle wood and spice in the backg rou nd. L a y e r e d , f u l l- b o d ie d , d e n s e, a nd opulent, it is nicely concentrated and yet exquisitely balanced with a long, satisfying finish. • 2019 Rockpile Zinfandel Jack’s Cabin Vineyard, $50 The Rockpile AVA is coming on strong as a producer of world class Zinfandel. Jack’s Cabin Vineyard is planted at 950 feet elevation and is a premier site. The wine made by the Mauritson family reveals copious quantities of earthy, smoky, toasty new oak notes along with saddle leather, and a perfumed mushroomy, blackberry scented nose. Drink this briery, perfumed, concentrated Zinfandel over the next 6 to 7 years. • 2019 Kokomo Zinfandel, $28 This wine from Sonoma’s Dry Creek Valley opens with a nose of cherries, raspberry preserves, and plu ms with hints of baking spices, licorice and chocolate. Big, rich and full-bodied, it packs in the dark fruit flavors with a firm, chewy frame and tons of tart freshness, finishing long and savory • 2020 Castoro Zinfusion The Udsen family started Castoro in 1983 making them one of the pioneer wineries in the Paso Robles area. The Zin grapes are supplemented with Petite Sirah, Primitivo and a splash of Tannat. It offers delicious red and black fruit, violets, herb and barbeque smoke characteristics as well as a lush easygoing mouthfeel finishing with a kiss of vanilla. • 2020 Trentadue La Storia Zinfandel This wine has been a “go to Zinfandel” for many years never failing to please. It is made by the talented winemaker Miro Tcholakov who also has his own label (Miro). This shows off chocolate and cherries notes with touches of prunes, earth, baking spices and raspberry jam. Full, rich, and opulent in the mouth it has stunning harmony with lots of layers and a rich satisfying finish. • 2018 Storrs Zinfandel Rusty Ridge, $34 Storrs has sourced these grapes from a series of old vine vineyards located on the eastern edge of the Santa Cruz Mountains. This area often gets overlooked in the stampede to acquire Napa and Sonoma wines but I find Santa Cruz to be every bit their equal in producing quality wine. The wine offers up copious notes of sweet boysenberry fruit, roasted herbs and a touch of vanilla. Lovely, pure, full-bodied and complex, as well as fresh and elegant, this vibrant, exuberant Zinfandel should drink well for up to 8 years. • 2019 Peachy Canyon Zinfandel Bailey Vineyard, $50 This wine hails from the Adelaida district in Paso Robles. The nose offers, crème de cassis, cherries and dusty soil. The palate is big and rich, full and fruity with blackberry pie, and plum flavors. The finish is long and savory and cries out for some BBQ pork ribs.

The finish is long and savory and cries out for some BBQ pork ribs. • 2019 Andis Zinfandel Grandpere Vineyard, $60 The famous Grandpere Vineyard was planted in the Sierra Foothills around 1869 and is still in production today. This rubyhued Zin offers briery, cherry, pepper, earth and wildflowers in the bouquet. Lots of blueberry and plum fruit on the medium bodied palate. Good acid and structure on the finish. • 2016 Green and Red Zinfandel Tip Top Vineyard, $42 Medium garnet-purple colored, the Tip Top Zin gives aromas of new leather, spice box, strawberries, and earth. Medium bodied with lots of dried berry and spice flavors on offer in the mouth, it has velvety tannins and plenty of freshness to harmonize and lift the finish. The fresh acidity would make it a great partner to Italian pasta dishes. • 2018 Quivira Black Boar Zinfandel, $55 Quivira is one of the standout wineries in Sonoma County’s Dry Creek Valley and the Black Boar is their premium zinfandel. It shows vivid black cherry and currant fruit notes intertwined with notions of lavender and spice. With a medium to full-bodied mouthfeel, a luscious, pure style, plenty of complexity and elegance. It is delicious now but should last for 7 or 8 years. • 2017 Alexander Valley Vineyards Redemption Zinfandel, $22 The theologically named Redemption Zin from Alexander Valley Vineyards has the varietal’s peppery, raspberry, and cherry fruit, earth and spice, and nice meatiness. It has great structure to support the ample black and red fruit, and a character that begs for some grilled tri-tip or flank steak. • 2018 Baca Zinfandel Home Base, $40 Jennifer Brown shepherds this new Zinfandel label which is part of the Hall family of wines. It is medium garnet-purple colored and opens with lovely potpourri and baking spice notes over a core of blueberry and plum fruit plus touches of dried herbs and leather. Opulently fruited with lots of spicy berry preserves flavors and a chewy frame, it has a good long, refreshing finish. • 2017 Bella Grace Zinfandel Estate, $34 This wine hails from Plymouth in Amador county in the Sierra foothills and I have had the pleasure to write about them before. The nose offers scents of blueberries, cinnamon, spice with notes of cherry preserves, soil and stone fruit aromas emerging with time in the glass. The palate is medium to full-bodied, with lush fruits and plush tannins finishing long and lifted. Great effort. • 2019 Gluntz Family Zinfandel Dante Dusi Vineyard, $40 The Dusi family owns some prime old vine Zinfandel Vineyards in Paso Robles and the Gluntz winery is the beneficiary of these prime grapes. The dense, thick, juicy 2019 Gluntz Zin displays a deep color. Ripe boysenberry and blueberry fruit intertwined with pepper and balsam wood notes are found in this long glycerin-imbued Zinfandel. It is so packed with fruit and flavor, no food is required – it is a meal in itself. • 2018 Hendry Zinfandel Block 28, $38 I have lost track of how many times Hendry has appeared in my list of top Zinfandels – their consistency is inspiring. The 2018 Block 28 Zin is an attractive, juicy wine layered with plums, dark red fruit and licorice. Hightoned and floral notes and a hint of pepper ad lift to the finish. This is a totally inviting, luscious red best enjoyed in its exuberant youth. • 2020 Florence Vineyard Zinfandel This is the first release under the Florence label for Jack Florence a grower in the Rockpile AVA. The debut offering offers blackberry and cassis notes with a subtle plum laced undercurrent plus spice box, black soil and floral hints. The concentrated medium-bodied palate is densely packed with dried berry and baking spice flavors with plush tannins and a lively lift to the finish. Future looks very promising. • 2019 Once and Future Zinfandel Oakley Road, $50 Most people don’t know that one of the best old vine Zinfandel vineyards in the entire state is in, of all places, Contra Costa County. The suburban town of Oakley boasts historic Zin vineyards planted a hundred years ago. Blackberry liqueur infused with smoke jumps from the glass of this delicious Zinfandel. Explosive in the mouth, with ample extract levels, fruit, and glycerin, but no heaviness or heat, this is an opulently textured luscious offering to drink over the 5-6 years. • 2019 Seghesio Zinfandel Home Ranch, $70 Seghesio’s Home Ranch Zinfandel is a perennial top performer at the ZAP tasting. The enormous bouquet of blackberries, chocolate, cherries, herbs, and coffee is as exotic as it is multidimensional. The wine exhibits opulently rich, expansive, full-bodied flavors oozing with extraction. This is a terrific, full-bodied voluptuously textured Zin for drinking over the next decade. • 2019 St. Francis Zinfandel Reserve, $45 Sonoma County’s St. Francis winery has put forth a compelling wine graced with expressive dark red fruit, flowers, mint, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries wrap around the finish. • 2019 Rombauer Zinfandel Twin Rivers, $42 The Twin Rivers Zin is medium garnet-purple colored and scented of crushed cherries blackberry pie with hints of Chinese five spice and dried herbs. Full-bodied, rich, and spicy in the mouth, it has a solid frame of soft tannins and a firm backbone, finishing long and peppery. • 2019 Trestle Glen Zinfandel This was my first introduction to Sonoma County’s Trestle Glen Winery. Their 2019 Zin reveals ripe blueberry and plum fruit with notions of spice and pepper in its fragrant, expressive bouquet. articles.text: Well-meaning family members and friends often give an enthusiastic “Yes!” when someone asks for a little help at home due to age, illness, or other life change that leaves them in need of support. It feels good to help someone out and make them happier, after all. However, this temporary commitment can soon expand into something that requires more than they can handle in terms of time, physical strength, or emotional stamina. Injured on the “Job” A family member may offer to help someone simply step safely out of the tub, and then find themselves with a back injury. There are proper techniques for lifting someone from a chair or bed, or assisting them in the bathroom, which professional caregivers receive training for. A possible solution is to determine which aspects of care seem the riskiest for the person who is helping out, then hire a caregiver to step in for those specific tasks instead. This might mean just an hour or two per day; giving the family member a little break and keeping them safe as well. What’s burnout? The definition of burnout is “fatigue, frustration, or apathy resulting from prolonged stress, overwork, or intense activity.” When an untrained family member or friend attempts to be a caregiver, while possibly balancing work or family responsibilities, they can burn out. It’s impossible to keep adding more and more to your plate, especially when you don’t really know what to do, or what’s coming next… Eventually the plate comes crashing down. Establishing boundaries is important for family caregivers so that they don’t experience burnout. If they’re not careful other issues can develop while caring for an elder loved one, such as stress at work or with children in the home. Consider asking other friends or family to share the responsibilities of caregiving or hire someone to be part of your care team. Feelings matter Caregivers can feel resentful, and it’s perfectly natural, especially if they give too much of themselves without much in return. Ideally, a care relationship can involve both give and take so that resentment doesn’t develop. Finding others who are having similar experiences can be helpful for negative feelings affecting a caregiver. There are all kinds of support groups, both online and in person, in which family caregivers can vent, learn, and share. Support groups might be for caregiving in general or for a specific type of caregiving such as for someone who is living with dementia or Parkinson’s disease. These groups may be an offshoot of an organization such as the Alzheimer’s Association or a local church. When a family member or friend begins to experience some of the possible challenges of caregiving, a professional caregiver can step in to ease the burden. Dear MacMama: I just got a MacBook Pro, and since I am not going into work, I have time to learn how to use it. I am coming from the PC world, so everything is different. Where do I start? –Leslie G., Oakland Dear Leslie: Congrats on your new purchase, and luckily, there are many good sources that provide information on becoming comfortable on the Mac platform. You can find help with books, online print sources, and videos. Here are some of my favorite sources. Books: I am still a page turning learner, and if I am learning something new, I like to sit with a highlighter and a book, and study like the old days! There are some excellent books on switching to Mac, whether you are a tech savvy user, or more of a beginner. The “For Dummies” series is excellent, and there is a “Switching to a Mac for Dummies”. Anything by David Pogue is great, although a bit more technical. One that I would strongly recommend is “macOS Catalina for Dummies” by Bob LeVitus. Also, the “for seniors” volumes are usually well written, specifically “Mac OS Catalina for Seniors” by Scott La Counte. Be aware that if these volumes are not current (2019 or later), the info might be outdated. Websites: Apple itself has a web page devoted to folks who switched to Mac from PCs: https://support.apple.com/en-us/ HT204216 You can find lots of good info here. I also really like the “How to Geek” (https://www. howtogeek.com/437168/how-toswitch-from-a-windows-pc-to-amac/). Another good source is wired. com. If you do a Google search “switching from PC to Mac” there are countless links from established sites Videos (YouTube): This is most likely your best bet. Anson Alexander has really good video series and his Mac tutorial for beginners is excellent (https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=67keaaWOKzE). Another good video is by macmost.com, including a video on “Questions New Mac Owners Have When Switching from Windows” (https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=vau_4NpkEB8). Of course, there are plenty of videos by helpful pros, and if you just got a new mac, you can always call AppleCare with any questions: 1-800-275-2273. I think you will find that there are many similarities, and the differences are mostly for power users. Of course, the file structure is different, and the user experience is also a bit different. If you are a photographer, artist or musician, you will appreciate the amount of software for you. And these days, the current version of Microsoft Office apps like Word and Excel are almost exactly the same on the Mac as PC. I would say that within a month or so you will feel like a pro. If you need more guidance, contact me, I am doing all of my support appointments remotely these days. articles.text: Tom Webster died at home in Piedmont peacefully, after a hemorrhagic stroke, surrounded by his family on February 26, 2022. He was 80 years old. Tom was born on January 13, 1942, in North Hollywood. The son of Phillip and Lilian Webster, he was the oldest of five children – brothers Calvin, John, and Bill and a sister, Barbara. Tom’s father was a mechanic and from the beginning of Tom’s life it was clear that he inherited his father’s genes. He had an insatiable desire to understand how things worked, both tangible and intangible. Tom started by getting in trouble for taking apart the family toasters and televisions when he was small, then moved on to working on cars throughout his youth and adolescence. Tom attended high school in Folsom, CA where he played football and cruised around in his 1955 Chevy. He was elected senior class president and was named Best All Around for the class of 1959. Tom graduated from UC Berkeley with a degree in Mechanical Engineering in 1964. After graduation, his best friend Ben Clawson, also a mechanical engineer, decided with Tom it was time for an adventure so they set out to build a sailboat. Six years later, Galatea, a 38-foot trimaran was finished and Tom, and Chris Weahunt – his girlfriend who became his wife of almost 50 years – and Ben started sailing adventures over a period of several years. The adventures took them down the coast of Mexico, out to Cocos Island, and onto the Galapagos where they were among the last group of private boats allowed to visit unaccompanied by a guide or organization. It was on these adventures, and especially time spent with Peace Corps volunteers in Central America where he became inspired to apply his engineering background to sustainable energy, moving onto the solar energy group at Lawrence Berkeley Lab (LBL). Tom and Chris were married for 48 years and had a loving and enduring relationship of 52 years. They went on many travels and adventures together over the years, from sailing trips, backTom Webster, a resident of Piedmont since 1993, died on February 26, 2022. He was 80. packing, travels through Central and South America, Europe, and numerous family vacations. They supported each other’s passions and interests and shared commitments of family, adventure, health, good food and wine, and sustainability. Tom was a loving, and committed father to two children, Brett (1982) and Kelsey (1986). Even through his busy and successful career of 53 years as an engineer, Tom made himself available to his children whenever they needed him – from before-school breakfasts, playing catch in the yard and attending ballet classes and performances, to lending a compassionate ear and shoulder to cry on, Tom was ever-present for his children. He and Chris made an excellent parenting team, something his children now attempt to emulate with their own children. Tom was the officiant at Kelsey and Nate’s wedding in 2014, as well as Brett and Laney’s in 2021. For the last years of his life, Tom was an exemplary grandfather (“Opa”) to Kelsey’s two children, Skylar (2017) and Hayden (2021). Laney is expecting a child this year, unfortunately one who won’t meet her Opa in person. Tom worked as an engineer initially for a few different companies before becoming a research engineer (upon return from his sailing adventures) for UC Berkeley. He worked at LBL (1976-1982) and Center for the Built Environment (CBE, 1995-2017), using a break from 1982-1995 to co-start an independent HVAC controls company, Energyline. Tom and his family moved to Piedmont in 1993 after their Oakland home was lost in the 1991 Oakland Hills fire. After his retirement from CBE, Tom became involved with Piedmont Connect, generously volunteering his engineering experience to help the City reduce greenhouse gas emissions. His meticulous energy and cost calculations and advocacy helped make plans for an all-electric city pool in Piedmont. In addition to engineering, Tom was very interested and dedicated to the study of Buddhism and spirituality. He began meditating and doing spiritual growth work in 1995, deepening and expanding his practice throughout the remainder of his life. He started following Adyashanti in 2005 and attended several silent retreats at Spirit Rock and Tassajara. Tom was a deeply kind, generous, loving person with a zest and energy for life that was unmatched. He made a lasting impact on people, whether they knew him for years or met him only briefly, with his genuine curiosity and interest in the well-being and goings-on of others. He had a rich and wonderful life, and he will be so sorely missed by all those who had the pleasure of knowing him, especially his family.
